claim: Volume-regulated anion channels (VRACs) are central to cell volume regulation.
source: Volume-regulated anion channels (VRACs) are central to cell volume regulation.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about VRAC function.

claim: VRACs are hetero-hexamers formed by LRRC8 proteins.
source: Recently identified as hetero-hexamers formed by LRRC8 proteins, their activation mechanism remains elusive.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge from recent literature about VRAC structure.

claim: Inter-subunit FRET from LRRC8 complexes tracked VRAC activation.
source: Inter-subunit FRET from LRRC8 complexes tracked VRAC activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The cytoplasmic domains of LRRC8 rearrange during VRAC opening.
source: With patch-clamp fluorometry, we confirmed that the cytoplasmic domains rearrange during VRAC opening.
evidence: This is confirmed by simultaneous patch-clamp and FRET measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Reduced intracellular ionic strength did not directly activate VRACs.
source: Reduced intracellular ionic strength did not directly activate VRACs, and VRACs were not activated on endomembranes.
evidence: This is supported by experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3 where VRACs in ER and Golgi did not respond to hypotonic treatment despite reduced ionic strength.

claim: VRACs were not activated on endomembranes.
source: Reduced intracellular ionic strength did not directly activate VRACs, and VRACs were not activated on endomembranes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments in Figures 2 and 3 showing no FRET response in ER and Golgi-localized VRACs.

claim: Pharmacological manipulation of diacylglycerol (DAG) activated or inhibited plasma membrane-localized VRACs.
source: Instead, pharmacological manipulation of diacylglycerol (DAG), and protein kinase D (PKD) activity, activated or inhibited plasma membrane-localized VRACs.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with PMA, DOG, and CRT 0066101 shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Pharmacological manipulation of protein kinase D (PKD) activity activated or inhibited plasma membrane-localized VRACs.
source: Instead, pharmacological manipulation of diacylglycerol (DAG), and protein kinase D (PKD) activity, activated or inhibited plasma membrane-localized VRACs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with PKD inhibitor CRT 0066101 shown in Figure 5.

claim: FRET detected robust activation of VRAC by PMA that was absent during whole-cell patch clamp.
source: Finally, we resolved previous contradictory reports concerning VRAC activation, using FRET to detect robust activation by PMA that was absent during whole-cell patch clamp.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 where PMA activates VRAC as measured by FRET but not during whole-cell patch clamp.

claim: VRACs are ubiquitously expressed and involved in regulatory volume decrease (RVD) of vertebrate cells.
source: Volume-regulated anion channels (VRACs) are ubiquitously expressed and involved in regulatory volume decrease (RVD) of vertebrate cells (Chen et al., 2019; Jentsch, 2016; Stauber, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: VRACs open slowly following osmotic cell swelling and mediate the extrusion of chloride and organic osmolytes, leading to the efflux of water and hence cell shrinkage.
source: These channels open slowly following osmotic cell swelling and mediate the extrusion of chloride and organic osmolytes, leading to the efflux of water and hence cell shrinkage.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VRAC function.

claim: VRACs are composed of LRRC8 heteromers containing the essential subunit LRRC8A and at least one other LRRC8 protein, LRRC8B-E.
source: VRACs are composed of LRRC8 heteromers containing the essential subunit LRRC8A and at least one other LRRC8 protein, LRRC8B-E (Qiu et al., 2014; Voss et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The subunit composition determines various biophysical properties and substrate permeability of VRACs.
source: The subunit composition determines various biophysical properties and substrate permeability (Planells-Cases et al., 2015; Syeda et al., 2016; Voss et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LRRC8A homomers can form anion channels, but with weak volume-sensitivity and very low conductance.
source: Although unlikely to be of physiological relevance, LRRC8A homomers can form anion channels, but with weak volume-sensitivity and very low conductance (Deneka et al., 2018; Syeda et al., 2016; Yamada and Strange, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LRRC8 proteins form hexamers with the N-terminal halves constituting the transmembrane domain of the channel complex with a single pore.
source: LRRC8 proteins form hexamers with the N-terminal halves of the six LRRC8 proteins constituting the transmembrane domain of the channel complex with a single pore.
evidence: This is established knowledge from structural studies.

claim: The C-terminal halves of LRRC8 proteins contain at least 16 leucine-rich repeats that form horseshoe-like structures reaching into the cytoplasm.
source: The C-terminal halves contain at least 16 leucine-rich repeats that form horseshoe-like structures reaching into the cytoplasm and their apparent flexibility has been hypothesized to be related to channel gating (Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The apparent flexibility of LRRC8 C-terminal domains has been hypothesized to be related to channel gating.
source: The C-terminal halves contain at least 16 leucine-rich repeats that form horseshoe-like structures reaching into the cytoplasm and their apparent flexibility has been hypothesized to be related to channel gating (Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous structural studies cited in the text.

claim: The reduction of intracellular ionic strength was reported to be crucial for VRAC activation upon osmotic cell swelling.
source: Notably, the reduction of intracellular ionic strength (Γi) was reported to be crucial for VRAC activation upon osmotic cell swelling (Voets et al., 1999) and reconstituted LRRC8 complexes in lipid bilayers could indeed be activated by low ionic strength (Syeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reconstituted LRRC8 complexes in lipid bilayers could be activated by low ionic strength.
source: Notably, the reduction of intracellular ionic strength (Γi) was reported to be crucial for VRAC activation upon osmotic cell swelling (Voets et al., 1999) and reconstituted LRRC8 complexes in lipid bilayers could indeed be activated by low ionic strength (Syeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: VRACs can be activated under iso-osmotic conditions that are unlikely to encompass any changes in intracellular ionic strength.
source: However, VRACs can also be activated under iso-osmotic conditions that are unlikely to encompass any changes in Γi (Pedersen et al., 2016; Strange et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In HeLa cells co-expressing CFP- and YFP tagged LRRC8A (A-CFP/A-YFP), bleaching of YFP robustly increased the intensity of CFP.
source: In HeLa cells co-expressing CFP- and YFP tagged LRRC8A (A-CFP/A-YFP), bleaching of YFP (the FRET acceptor) robustly increased the intensity of CFP (the FRET donor), compared to unbleached cells in the same field of view (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: FRET was observed when LRRC8A was combined with LRRC8E (A-CFP/E-YFP or A-YFP/E-CFP).
source: The same was observed when LRRC8A was combined with the VRAC subunit LRRC8E (A-CFP/E-YFP or A-YFP/E-CFP), but not when combined with plasma membrane-localized CD4-YFP, used as control for FRET by membrane crowding (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No FRET was observed when LRRC8A was combined with plasma membrane-localized CD4-YFP.
source: The same was observed when LRRC8A was combined with the VRAC subunit LRRC8E (A-CFP/E-YFP or A-YFP/E-CFP), but not when combined with plasma membrane-localized CD4-YFP, used as control for FRET by membrane crowding (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The C-termini of LRRC8 proteins are within FRET distance (~5 nm) for the fluorescent protein adjuncts, irrespective of VRAC subunit composition.
source: Therefore, irrespective of VRAC subunit composition, the C-termini are within FRET distance for the fluorescent protein adjuncts (~5 nm).
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Switching from isotonic to hypotonic buffer led to a robust decrease in cFRET by 5–10% within 90 s in both HeLa and HEK293 cells expressing A-CFP/E-YFP.
source: Switching from isotonic (340 mOsm) to hypotonic (250 mOsm) buffer led to a robust decrease in cFRET by 5–10% within 90 s in both HeLa and HEK293 cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The intra-molecular cFRET of a cytosolic tandem FRET pair construct, CFP-18aa-YFP, was unaffected by hypotonic buffer.
source: In contrast, the intra-molecular cFRET of a cytosolic tandem FRET pair construct, CFP-18aa-YFP (Elder et al., 2009), and of a plasma membrane-localized ionotropic glutamate receptor (Zachariassen et al., 2016) were unaffected by hypotonic buffer (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cFRET of a plasma membrane-localized ionotropic glutamate receptor was unaffected by hypotonic buffer.
source: In contrast, the intra-molecular cFRET of a cytosolic tandem FRET pair construct, CFP-18aa-YFP (Elder et al., 2009), and of a plasma membrane-localized ionotropic glutamate receptor (Zachariassen et al., 2016) were unaffected by hypotonic buffer (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The kinetics of the cFRET drop and its reversibility correlated with the activation and inactivation of hypotonicity-induced VRAC-mediated anion currents.
source: The kinetics of the cFRET drop and its reversibility correlated with the activation and inactivation of hypotonicity-induced VRAC-mediated anion currents (Figure 1F), demonstrating that the cFRET decrease indeed reflects VRAC opening.
evidence: This is supported by simultaneous patch-clamp and FRET measurements shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A progressive decrease in cFRET accompanied additional hypotonicity.
source: A progressive decrease in cFRET accompanied additional hypotonicity but, again mirroring VRAC, cFRET did not increase with hypertonic treatment (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: cFRET did not increase with hypertonic treatment.
source: A progressive decrease in cFRET accompanied additional hypotonicity but, again mirroring VRAC, cFRET did not increase with hypertonic treatment (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Relative changes in cFRET did not depend on the A-CFP/E-YFP expression ratio.
source: We did not see a correlation between intensity of CFP or YFP and absolute cFRET values (not shown), neither did relative changes in cFRET depend on the A-CFP/E-YFP expression ratio (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: cFRET decreased for A-CFP/A-YFP constructs, providing evidence for activation of homomeric LRRC8A complexes in a cellular context.
source: Remarkably, cFRET also decreased for A-CFP/A-YFP constructs (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), providing evidence for activation of homomeric LRRC8A complexes in a cellular context.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The RD sensor indicated a reversible decrease in intracellular ionic strength in HeLa cells during hypotonic treatment.
source: As expected, this sensor indicated a reversible decrease in Γi in HeLa cells during hypotonic treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The decrease in intracellular ionic strength was homogeneous over the entire cell volume during hypotonic treatment.
source: Notably, the decrease was homogeneous over the entire cell volume (Figure 2B, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ER-trapped VRACs did not respond to hypotonic treatment.
source: However, ER-trapped VRACs surprisingly did not respond to hypotonic treatment (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutation of the LRRC8A N-glycosylation sites did not impinge on the activation-dependent cFRET drop at the plasma membrane.
source: This was likely not due to incomplete glycosylation since mutation of the LRRC8A N-glycosylation sites (Voss et al., 2014) did not impinge on the activation-dependent cFRET drop at the plasma membrane (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ER-localized A-CFP-FM2/E-YFP VRAC did not respond to application of hypotonic buffer.
source: Concurrent sensitized FRET measurements showed that neither ER-localized (at 10 min) nor Golgi-localized (80 min) A-CFP-FM2/E-YFP VRAC responded to application of hypotonic buffer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Golgi-localized A-CFP-FM2/E-YFP VRAC did not respond to application of hypotonic buffer.
source: Concurrent sensitized FRET measurements showed that neither ER-localized (at 10 min) nor Golgi-localized (80 min) A-CFP-FM2/E-YFP VRAC responded to application of hypotonic buffer.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: cFRET was reduced for A-CFP-FM2/E-YFP that had reached the plasma membrane after 165 min.
source: On the other hand, as expected, cFRET was reduced for A-CFP-FM2/E-YFP that had reached the plasma membrane after 165 min (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Despite hypotonic treatment reducing intracellular ionic strength homogenously over the whole cell, VRACs are only activated when they reach the plasma membrane.
source: Thus, despite hypotonic treatment reducing Γi homogenously over the whole cell, VRACs are only activated when they reach the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Depolymerization of the actin cytoskeleton by latrunculin B did not alter VRAC activation by ~25% hypotonicity.
source: In agreement with earlier reports on ICl,swell in lymphocytes (Levitan et al., 1995), depolymerization of the actin cytoskeleton by latrunculin B did not alter VRAC activation by ~25% hypotonicity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Cholesterol depletion by methyl-β-cyclodextrin potentiated VRAC activation.
source: In contrast, cholesterol depletion by methyl-β-cyclodextrin potentiated VRAC activation, as judged by the reduction in cFRET (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C), as was previously shown for VRAC-mediated ICl,swell in bovine aortic endothelial cells (Levitan et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: In isotonic conditions, PMA evoked a robust decrease in cFRET in HeLa and HEK293 cells expressing A-CFP/A-YFP or A-CFP/E-YFP.
source: In isotonic conditions, PMA evoked a robust decrease in cFRET in HeLa and HEK293 cells expressing A-CFP/A-YFP or A-CFP/E-YFP (Figure 4A), but not CFP-18aa-YFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PMA did not evoke a decrease in cFRET in cells expressing CFP-18aa-YFP.
source: In isotonic conditions, PMA evoked a robust decrease in cFRET in HeLa and HEK293 cells expressing A-CFP/A-YFP or A-CFP/E-YFP (Figure 4A), but not CFP-18aa-YFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Subsequent inactivation of VRAC by treatment with hyper-osmotic solution restored basal FRET levels after PMA activation.
source: This reflects gating of the LRRC8 complex, because subsequent inactivation of VRAC by treatment with hyper-osmotic solution restored basal FRET levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Activation by PMA required cell surface localization, as VRACs released from aggregation were immune to PMA in the ER and Golgi.
source: Like hypotonicity-driven VRAC activation, activation by PMA required cell surface localization, as VRACs released from aggregation were immune to PMA in the ER and Golgi, but they were activated at the plasma membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: VRACs released from aggregation were activated by PMA at the plasma membrane.
source: Like hypotonicity-driven VRAC activation, activation by PMA required cell surface localization, as VRACs released from aggregation were immune to PMA in the ER and Golgi, but they were activated at the plasma membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Recording HEK293 KO cells expressing A-CFP/E-YFP in whole-cell voltage-clamp configuration, no FRET reduction was detected upon PMA application.
source: Surprisingly, recording HEK293 KO cells expressing A-CFP/E-YFP in whole-cell voltage-clamp configuration, we could no longer detect any FRET reduction, nor did PMA activate VRAC currents (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PMA did not activate VRAC currents in HEK293 KO cells expressing A-CFP/E-YFP during whole-cell voltage-clamp.
source: Surprisingly, recording HEK293 KO cells expressing A-CFP/E-YFP in whole-cell voltage-clamp configuration, we could no longer detect any FRET reduction, nor did PMA activate VRAC currents (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Incubating HEK293 KO cells expressing A-CFP/E-YFP with PMA before membrane breakthrough resulted in a reliable increase in classical VRAC currents.
source: Indeed, with this experimental design we observed a reliable increase in classical VRAC currents in HEK293 KO cells expressing A-CFP/E-YFP incubated with PMA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The whole-cell voltage-clamp configuration affects signaling pathways involved in activation of VRAC in a time-dependent manner.
source: This result demonstrates that the whole-cell voltage-clamp configuration affects signaling pathways involved in activation of VRAC in a time-dependent manner, an experimental caveat that can be overcome with our non-invasive FRET sensor.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The PKC inhibitor Gö6983 prevented the cFRET reduction upon hypotonicity.
source: Using the PKC inhibitor Gö6983 not only prevented the cFRET reduction upon hypotonicity, it also gradually increased cFRET over the course of the experiment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The PKC inhibitor Gö6983 gradually increased cFRET over the course of the experiment.
source: Using the PKC inhibitor Gö6983 not only prevented the cFRET reduction upon hypotonicity, it also gradually increased cFRET over the course of the experiment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: In the whole-cell patch-clamp configuration, the hypotonicity-induced current persisted in isotonic buffer when supplemented with Gö6983.
source: However, in the whole-cell patch-clamp configuration, the hypotonicity-induced current even persisted in isotonic buffer when supplemented with Gö6983 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The presence of the PKD inhibitor CRT 0066101 during hypotonic treatment abolished cFRET changes.
source: The presence of the PKD inhibitor CRT 0066101 during hypotonic treatment abolished cFRET changes and strongly reduced VRAC currents in HEK293 KO cells expressing A-CFP/E-YFP (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The presence of the PKD inhibitor CRT 0066101 during hypotonic treatment strongly reduced VRAC currents in HEK293 KO cells expressing A-CFP/E-YFP.
source: The presence of the PKD inhibitor CRT 0066101 during hypotonic treatment abolished cFRET changes and strongly reduced VRAC currents in HEK293 KO cells expressing A-CFP/E-YFP (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The presence of CRT 0066101 readily diminished currents following breakthrough after pre-incubation in hypotonic buffer.
source: Similar to incubation during the whole-cell patch-clamp experiment, the presence of CRT 0066101 readily diminished currents following breakthrough after pre-incubation in hypotonic buffer, whereas Gö6983 did not (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Gö6983 did not diminish currents following breakthrough after pre-incubation in hypotonic buffer.
source: Similar to incubation during the whole-cell patch-clamp experiment, the presence of CRT 0066101 readily diminished currents following breakthrough after pre-incubation in hypotonic buffer, whereas Gö6983 did not (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DAG-activated PKD plays an essential role in hypotonicity-induced VRAC activation.
source: This suggests an essential role of DAG-activated PKD in hypotonicity-induced VRAC activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments with PKD inhibitor shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: In the presence of DOG, a persistent VRAC current was observed after switching from extracellular hypotonicity to normal, isotonic buffer for A-CFP/E-YFP expressed in HEK293 KO cells.
source: Indeed, in the presence of DOG, we observed a persistent VRAC current after switching from extracellular hypotonicity to normal, isotonic buffer for A-CFP/E-YFP expressed in HEK293 KO cells (Figure 5C, left panel, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, left panel), as well as for endogenous VRAC in WT HEK293 cells (Figure 5C, right panel, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the presence of DOG, a persistent VRAC current was observed after switching from extracellular hypotonicity to normal, isotonic buffer for endogenous VRAC in WT HEK293 cells.
source: Indeed, in the presence of DOG, we observed a persistent VRAC current after switching from extracellular hypotonicity to normal, isotonic buffer for A-CFP/E-YFP expressed in HEK293 KO cells (Figure 5C, left panel, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, left panel), as well as for endogenous VRAC in WT HEK293 cells (Figure 5C, right panel, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The DGK inhibitor DOG impaired the recovery of cFRET to basal values when cells were returned to isotonicity after hypotonic treatment.
source: For the A-CFP/E-YFP VRAC expressed in either HEK293 KO cells in whole-cell patch clamp (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, left panel) and non-dialyzed HeLa cells (Figure 5D, left panel, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) the DGK inhibitor DOG impaired the recovery of cFRET to basal values when cells were returned to isotonicity after hypotonic treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Intracellular ionic strength fully recovered to normal levels irrespective of the presence of DOG.
source: In striking contrast, Γi fully recovered to the normal levels irrespective of the presence of DOG (Figure 2A, Figure 5D, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 5D.

claim: Opening of VRACs is not directly coupled to intracellular ionic strength, but rather to the DAG pathway, likely through activation of PKD in HeLa and HEK293 cells.
source: These results demonstrate that opening of VRACs is not directly coupled to Γi, but rather to the DAG pathway, likely through activation of PKD in HeLa and HEK293 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The reversible decrease in FRET matches reversible VRAC activation upon treatment with hypo-osmotic solutions.
source: Here we present an intra-complex FRET sensor to monitor VRAC activity in live cells with subcellular resolution. The relationship of the observed FRET changes to VRAC gating are clear from numerous common features (Akita and Okada, 2014; König and Stauber, 2019; Pedersen et al., 2016; Strange et al., 2019): (i) the reversible decrease in FRET matches reversible VRAC activation upon treatment with hypo-osmotic solutions, and with the same kinetics as simultaneously-measured whole-cell VRAC currents
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in the study and cited literature.

claim: The intensity of the FRET decrease correlates with the applied extracellular hypotonicity.
source: (ii) the intensity of the FRET decrease correlates with the applied extracellular hypotonicity
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The modulation of VRAC currents by cholesterol depletion is mirrored by the observed FRET alteration.
source: (iii) the modulation of VRAC currents, for example by cholesterol depletion, is mirrored by the observed FRET alteration
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: After activation with PMA, FRET rises in hypertonicity as VRAC is inactivated by cell shrinkage.
source: (iv) after activation with PMA, FRET rises in hypertonicity as VRAC is inactivated by cell shrinkage.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FRET sensors unrelated to VRAC are not affected by hypo-osmotic solutions.
source: FRET sensors unrelated to VRAC are not affected by hypo-osmotic solutions, demonstrating that the observed changes with our FRET sensor are indeed specific for VRAC activation.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The activation of low-conducting VRACs composed of only LRRC8A could be detected by FRET.
source: The activation of low-conducting VRACs composed of only LRRC8A (Deneka et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Syeda et al., 2016; Yamada and Strange, 2018) could also be detected by FRET.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cryo-EM structures of VRAC complexes suggest a certain flexibility of their C-terminal leucine-rich domains (LRRDs) on the intracellular side.
source: Cryo-EM structures of VRAC complexes suggest a certain flexibility of their C-terminal leucine-rich domains (LRRDs) on the intracellular side. Related conformational rearrangements might be related to channel gating (Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: A decrease in FRET between fluorophores at the C-termini of LRRC8 proteins upon VRAC activation may reflect a displacement of LRRDs or possibly a simple change in the average orientation of the fluorophores to each other.
source: In support of this idea, we observe a decrease in FRET between fluorophores at the C-termini of LRRC8 proteins upon VRAC activation, which may reflect a displacement of LRRDs or possibly a simple change in the average orientation of the fluorophores to each other.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data and structural knowledge.

claim: Changes in FRET demonstrate movement of the cytosolic domains during VRAC activation, as has been shown for other ion channels.
source: Thus, as has previously been shown for cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channels (Zheng and Zagotta, 2000), slow gating of CLC chloride channels (Bykova et al., 2006), BK potassium channels (Miranda et al., 2013) and ionotropic glutamate receptors (Zachariassen et al., 2016), changes in FRET demonstrate movement of the cytosolic domains during VRAC activation.
evidence: This is supported by the data in this study and citations to previous studies on other channels.

claim: VRACs were previously shown to be directly activated by low ionic strength in lipid bilayer reconstitution.
source: VRACs were previously shown to be directly activated by low ionic strength in lipid bilayer reconstitution (Syeda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: When cells were treated with the DAG kinase inhibitor DOG, VRAC remained active in isotonic buffer after activation by hypotonicity, even though intracellular ionic strength recovered to normal levels.
source: However, we find that reduced Γi is neither sufficient to activate VRAC on intracellular compartments, nor is it indispensable to keep plasma membrane-localized VRACs active. When cells were treated with the DAG kinase inhibitor DOG, VRAC remained active in isotonic buffer after activation by hypotonicity, even though Γi recovered to normal levels.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Several studies reported VRAC activation when isotonic fluid was injected into, or inactivation when fluid was withdrawn from the cells without altering the intracellular ionic strength.
source: Several studies reported VRAC activation when isotonic fluid was injected into, or inactivation when fluid was withdrawn from the cells without altering the intracellular ionic strength (Best and Brown, 2009; Cannon et al., 1998; Poletto Chaves and Varanda, 2008; Zhang and Lieberman, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The extents of low ionic strength required for VRAC activation are unlikely to occur in physiological conditions or during whole-cell current measurements routinely used to study hypotonicity-induced VRAC currents.
source: Moreover, the extents of low ionic strength required for VRAC activation (Cannon et al., 1998; Deneka et al., 2018; Nilius et al., 1998; Syeda et al., 2016) are unlikely to occur in physiological conditions or during whole-cell current measurements routinely used to study hypotonicity-induced VRAC currents (Strange et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A putative role for ionic strength in controlling the volume set point for VRAC activation would be consistent with the findings of this study.
source: Instead, a putative role for ionic strength in controlling the volume set point for VRAC activation (Best and Brown, 2009; Cannon et al., 1998; Jackson et al., 1996) would be consistent with our findings.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Application of PMA led to VRAC opening even under isotonic conditions.
source: Rather than ionic strength, we observe a specific and potent action of the DAG-PKD pathway in VRAC activation. Application of PMA led to VRAC opening even under isotonic conditions and VRACs did not inactivate completely in isotonic buffer after activation by hypotonicity when the consumption of DAG by DAG kinase was inhibited.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: VRACs did not inactivate completely in isotonic buffer after activation by hypotonicity when the consumption of DAG by DAG kinase was inhibited.
source: Rather than ionic strength, we observe a specific and potent action of the DAG-PKD pathway in VRAC activation. Application of PMA led to VRAC opening even under isotonic conditions and VRACs did not inactivate completely in isotonic buffer after activation by hypotonicity when the consumption of DAG by DAG kinase was inhibited.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A role for DAG, which is generated by the activity of phospholipases C (PLCs), in the signaling for VRAC activation has been reported previously.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There are multiple contradictory reports on the involvement of DAG-activated PKCs in VRAC activation.
source: However, there are multiple contradictory reports on the involvement of DAG-activated PKCs.

claim: In some studies, PKCs were shown to be required for regulatory volume decrease.

claim: Other studies found no role for PKC despite a VRAC-activating effect of DAG.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The data do not support a core role for PKC in VRAC activation.
source: While our data speak against a core role for PKC in VRAC activation, they do not rule out a regulatory role for this kinase family.

claim: Protein kinase D (PKD) activity is critically involved in hypotonicity-induced activation of VRAC.
source: Instead, our experiments reveal that protein kinase D (PKD) activity is critically involved in hypotonicity-induced activation of VRAC.
